items.title: NA health panel visits Pims, says fire in nursery may have been caused by 'technical fault'
items.description: Members of the National Assembly’s Standing Committee on National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination said on Thursday that the fire at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), which claimed the lives of 14 infants, may have been caused by a “technical fault”. Health Minister Mustafa Kamal had attributed Wednesday’s incident to a spark in the air conditioner. But standing committee chairperson Mahesh Kumar Malani told the media in Islamabad on Thursday that “we have to see whether the fire was the result of negligence or a natural cause. It appears that there may have been a technical fault”. He added that the source of the fire had yet to be ascertained. “Some said that a spark was caused by an old air conditioner, [but] it had not been working for some time. The other two were portable,” he said. Malani said one of the doctors had stated that a spark was caused by a bundle of wires while the nurses said it all happened suddenly. “So no one saw where the spark came from. We have concluded that no one knows the source of the fire,” he said. He recalled it was earlier stated that the presence of oxygen caused the fire to spread, adding that it was possible that there was a fault in the oxygen pipes. However, “one thing is final, no one knows the source of the fire”, he reiterated, adding that the hospital’s executive director also agreed that the spark had not originated from the air conditioner. “Nevertheless, there was a fault (somewhere),” Malani continued, suggesting that it could either have been in “oxygen pipes or the electricity wiring”. He noted that the nursery where the incident took place was built in 1990 and stressed that there should not have been a nursery in the old building, particularly when there was a newly built block available on the premises. “The nursery was not fit for the babies. This was supposed to be a gynae ward, and the babies should have been kept in the new block which was well-equipped,” he said. Malani told reporters that the standing committee had sought answers from the hospital administration on certain questions. “We are calling a committee meeting and will look at the issue on the grounds of merit,” he said, adding that the committee would also study the findings to be presented by a separate inquiry committee formed by Prime Minister Shehbaz within 24-48 hours. Standing next to Malani, Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party MNA Gul Asghar Khan said, “We have also asked Pims how often fire drills are carried out in the hospital and when the last drill was conducted.” He added that the committee had also sought information on Pims’ last fire audit as well as human errors which may have led to the incident. PPP MNA Shazia Sobia Aslam Soomro added that the committee had also requested information on the functionality of fire alarms at the hospital. Taking note of “conflicting statements” by the staff, she said they suggested that “either there was no one on duty, or if they were on duty, they were somewhere outside”. She demanded that the Pims executive director, as well as the health minister, step down on “moral grounds”. Responding to a question, Malani said that “technical experts” should also be consulted in determining the cause of the fire. He, too, took note of the conflicting accounts by the staff. “The gynae head told me that there was a bundle of wires in the ward, while someone said there may have been an oxygen cylinder that exploded”, he said, adding, “How could an oxygen cylinder have exploded when there weren’t any?” So, the source of the fire was not yet known, he said. Malani said the committee would examine “whether the right person was appointed for the right job” to ascertain any technical faults. Committee member Farakh Khan also spoke on the occasion and raised concerns about whether the nursery had undergone any maintenance over the years. “If any maintenance had been carried out, why was an old air conditioner still installed in the room and why was the wiring left exposed?” she questioned, adding that if the administration could not manage the nursery, “they should finish it off”. Malani then said the committee had sought information on the budget of Pims’ Mother and Child Health Care Centre, and details about “how much of it was utilised”. He said details about the number of times the oxygen and electricity systems were examined had specifically been sought. Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl MNA Aliya Kamran said when the committee members spoke to the nurses, “it appeared as if they had been told what to say”. She said the staff had left the infants unattended as the fire broke out. “We are also not satisfied with the account the doctor on duty gave us,” she added. She claimed there was a “deliberate attempt” to push the narrative that the blaze had originated from the air conditioner. Kamran said that the NA committee would call the hospital administration and “question them within our capacity and present a fair opinion”. Echoing her fellows’ remarks, Kamran demanded that the health minister resign. “The inquiry team will not be able to maintain transparency if he is in power,” she said and demanded that the on-duty staff be suspended and their medical licences be revoked. Fire at Pims On Wednesday, 14 babies died after a fire erupted in Mother and Child Hospital’s ward at Pims. At the time, the health minister claimed that the fire began with a spark in the AC, while the bereaved families said the rescue teams arrived too late. According to a statement by the hospital, the incident was “initially caused by a spark inside nursery at 06:38am and within seconds a massive fire erupted due to oxygen points at each incubator”. It said two doctors and two nurses on duty inside the nursery responded “immediately and called security staff, who joined in and tried to get in twice [to bring] babies out until 06:39am, when a huge blast occurred and ceilings fell down”. Several witnesses, their hands and faces blackened from the smoke, told AFP they waited hours for help from the emergency services and were forced to smash through windows to get to the ward while some found the doors locked — an account the hospital and government later denied. Soon after the incident, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed an inquiry committee and removed federal Health Secretary Muhammad Aslam Ghauri. Meanwhile, a notification issued by the Islamabad district magistrate said that a seven-member fact-finding committee, headed by the additional deputy commissioner general (ADCG), had been formed to determine the facts behind the fire. Speaking to reporters in Islamabad on Wednesday, the health minister said he will present himself to his superiors for accountability. He said the incident was being investigated by “experts, different institutions including us”, adding that “nothing will remain hidden and all facts will be unearthed”. The incident has sparked outrage across the political spectrum, with many demanding accountability and criticising the hospital administration.

items.title: Chaleur en entreprise | L’équipement compte autant que le programme
items.description: Un événement d’entreprise prévu six mois à l’avance ne peut pas anticiper la météo du jour. Ce qu’il peut anticiper, c’est le matériel : où trouver de l’ombre, comment distribuer l’eau, et ce que chacun aura entre les mains pendant les heures les plus chaudes. Les autorités sanitaires recommandent souvent de boire régulièrement avant même de ressentir la soif et de privilégier les activités douces pendant les fortes chaleurs. Cette consigne, simple sur le papier, se heurte souvent à un problème logistique : un point d’eau mal placé n’est tout simplement pas utilisé. Le matériel dépend du programme, pas l’inverse Un déjeuner sur une terrasse et une après-midi au bord d’un lac n’appellent pas le même équipement. Pour une activité aquatique, chaque participant doit savoir ce qu’il apporte et ce qui est fourni sur place. Des Serviettes de plage personnalisées de Loopper peuvent par exemple servir à identifier le linge distribué à chaque équipe et à éviter les échanges entre participants. Le choix d’un tel objet se fait sur des critères concrets : taille, absorption, temps de séchage, conditions de lavage. Le marquage répond à un besoin d’organisation, pas l’inverse. Un objet choisi uniquement parce qu’il est facile à distribuer finit souvent dans un sac, oublié dès le retour au bureau. Ce que reçoivent les participants doit servir à quelque chose La même logique s’applique à tout objet remis en fin de journée. Les cadeaux d’entreprise ont davantage de sens lorsqu’ils correspondent à l’activité vécue ou répondent à un besoin identifié sur place, plutôt qu'à un choix générique. Quatre questions permettent de trancher avant toute commande : ● À quel moment l’objet sera-t-il utilisé ? ● Les participants doivent-ils le transporter toute la journée ? ● Remplace-t-il quelque chose qu’ils auraient dû apporter eux-mêmes ? ● Sera-t-il encore utile après l’événement ? Ces questions évitent de transformer une attention en contrainte supplémentaire pour l’invité. Les équipes présentes sur place sont exposées plus longtemps Les participants arrivent une fois l’installation terminée. Les techniciens, traiteurs et équipes d’accueil, eux, travaillent déjà depuis plusieurs heures, souvent avec un effort physique que les invités ne voient pas : monter du mobilier, transporter du matériel, installer une scène. L’INRS recommande, pour ces situations, d’augmenter la fréquence des pauses, de fournir une source d’eau fraîche et d’aménager de véritables espaces de repos. Une ouverture au public à neuf heures peut ainsi imposer une installation dès six heures, avec les mêmes besoins en ombre et en eau qui doivent être disponibles à ce moment-là, avant même l’arrivée du premier invité. Le bilan porte sur l’usage, pas sur le confort ressenti Une journée sans coup de chaud ne prouve pas que le dispositif était bien pensé. Le bilan utile porte sur des faits vérifiables : quantité d’eau réellement consommée, zones d’ombre les plus fréquentées, matériel utilisé ou resté dans les cartons. La vigilance canicule de Météo-France donne un cadre objectif pour fixer, en amont, le seuil à partir duquel le programme doit changer. Poser cette limite avant l’envoi des invitations évite d’improviser une décision une heure avant l’arrivée des premiers participants. L’article Chaleur en entreprise | L’équipement compte autant que le programme est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Not American Enough
items.description: F or Carlos Alemán , the pinnacle of the dozen years since he became a U.S. citizen was the night in 2020 when he was elected to serve on the city council of Homewood, Alabama. One of the lowest moments came earlier this year, when he learned that some of the most powerful people in his state are attempting to ban immigrants like him from pursuing higher office. “It seems to be part of a project to reject anyone who’s not born in this country as not worthy or deserving of the full rights of citizenship,” Alemán, who was born in Nicaragua, told me. For most of American history, becoming a citizen has meant acquiring the right to participate in virtually all aspects of civic life, including voting, serving on juries, and mounting a campaign for any political office other than the presidency. But in Alabama and other states across the country, Republican lawmakers are now pushing to make an important distinction: Naturalized citizens, they argue, should not have the same right to serve in public office as someone born in the United States. In recent months, an idea once confined to the fringes has gained mainstream traction across the country. Republican legislators in several states have introduced proposals that would restrict naturalized citizens and dual citizens from running for a range of elected positions, including sheriff and governor. In Congress, at least five Republicans have sponsored various proposals to bar naturalized or dual citizens from serving in roles including federal judgeships, Cabinet posts, and ambassadorships, and in Congress itself. Florida lawmakers this year enacted a law requiring candidates for several state and federal offices to disclose whether they hold another citizenship in addition to being a citizen of the United States. The movement has been fueled in part by the rise of a new class of foreign-born politicians—most prominently New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Ugandan-born son of parents of Indian extraction, whose ascent has become a favorite target of the right. His victory, along with the success of other progressive candidates born outside the U.S., has come to symbolize something dangerous in the eyes of President Trump’s MAGA base: the ability of people born elsewhere to acquire American citizenship and the possibility of political power. Now Republican lawmakers are pledging to do something about it. The push began in parallel to Mamdani’s rise. When Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen first floated the idea of barring naturalized citizens from serving in elected office, he cited Mamdani’s mayoral run as one impetus. “We want to make sure that no potential foreign influence or foreign meddling could impact our state’s highest elected leaders,” he told AL.com last year. Trump’s June defeat at the Supreme Court on birthright citizenship has also been a motivating factor. After his administration failed to convince a majority of the justices that his executive order limiting citizenship for those born in the U.S. to undocumented parents was constitutional, Trump wrote on social media that he would find alternative routes to accomplish his goals “in Congress through Legislation.” Drawing on the president’s “America First” rhetoric, some Trump allies have begun targeting the political rights of naturalized citizens in a broad campaign to continue that fight. “Even as we have progressed technologically, Immigration Policy has eroded those gains and living conditions for many,” Trump wrote last November on Truth Social, pledging to permanently pause migration from developing countries and denaturalize immigrants he deemed disruptive. “Only REVERSE MIGRATION can fully cure this situation. Other than that, HAPPY THANKSGIVING TO ALL, except those that hate, steal, murder, and destroy everything that America stands for—You won’t be here for long!” T rump used to strike a different tone when talking about naturalized Americans. In 2019, Trump welcomed five legal immigrants into the White House, hailing the “beauty and majesty of citizenship” as he conducted what he described as the first-ever naturalization ceremony in the Oval Office. “No matter where our story begins, whether we are the first generation or the tenth generation, we are all equal,” Trump told the new Americans. During the Republican National Convention the following year, the president again used the trappings of the White House to swear in new citizens and praise them for earning their status the proper way. “With the rights and freedoms each of you now enjoy as citizens, there is no dream beyond your wildest reach,” he said. The president, and the party he leads, have since soured on such inclusive rhetoric about America as a melting pot where everyone is equal and anyone can achieve anything. For a more up-to-date sense of how the president views America’s legal-immigration process, one need look no further than his Truth Social account. “If you import The Third World, you become The Third World!” he posted in April. A few weeks later, he reposted an anti-immigrant screed from a right-wing podcaster that questioned the loyalty of naturalized Americans and declared that “the idea of the melting pot is long over.” This narrative shift is showing up in policy as well. An analysis in January found that the Trump administration’s restrictive immigration policies would reduce legal immigration by one-third to one-half over his four-year term, affecting 1.5 million to 2.4 million people. The campaign to bar naturalized citizens from public office is a lesser-known manifestation of this broader push. Although the Constitution has always required aspirants for the presidency—and, by extension, the vice presidency—to be “a natural born Citizen,” it makes no such demand for any other government position. Some Republicans are now seeking to change that. State lawmakers in Alabama introduced legislation earlier this year that would require natural-born citizenship of those seeking to run for governor, legislator, sheriff, or a handful of other elected positions. Republican legislators introduced similar bills in Kentucky and Tennessee this year. Although the proposals—which face significant constitutional questions—have not yet passed, the effort is nevertheless building momentum. When the law in Florida requiring disclosure for dual citizens takes effect next year, it will mark the first time such a proposal has become state law. Many Republican-base voters have taken a sharp turn against legal immigration in recent years, in some cases even outpacing Trump himself in their rebellion against foreigners’ influence on American culture and commerce. The kind of racist rhetoric the president has long used against undocumented immigrants from developing nations—“They’re poisoning the blood of our country,” Trump said in 2023—is now regularly being directed against legal immigrants too. Last week, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, said that he would bar public schools in his state from hiring H-1B-visa holders. He described the first-of-its-kind proposal as a way to reduce “foreign influence” and “indoctrination in the classroom.” That push has dovetailed with the ascendance of Mamdani and other liberal, foreign-born politicians. The combination of their leftist views and their status as naturalized Americans has provided fodder for right-wing voices who have tried to blame America’s immigration policies and increased diversity for a growing list of the country’s problems. Representative Nancy Mace—who has introduced resolutions this year seeking to disqualify naturalized citizens and dual citizens from serving in Congress, the federal judiciary, and dozens of federal offices—has pointed to her left-leaning colleagues as motivation. [ Read: Mamdani is the foil Trump wants ] “We have been called racist, xenophobic and hateful,” she wrote in a Newsweek op-ed that was published on the nation’s 250th birthday. “But when you see a pattern of foreign-born officials who have proven time and again they are not America First, what is wrong with wanting them out of power?” Mace told me that because the actions of members of Congress have “enormous consequences” for national security, “the American people deserve to know the people holding them have one allegiance: America.” She did not say what specific risks her proposals would address. According to congressional records, 26 House members and six Senators were born outside the U.S., though some were born to American parents living abroad. Democrats dominate the list, but there are several Republicans who hail from other nations, including Cuba, Ukraine, and Mexico. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, a Republican who was born in Colombia and became a U.S. citizen when he turned 18, will be barred from serving if Mace’s proposal becomes law. But he has introduced legislation of his own that aims to crack down on the concept of dual citizenship, proposing to ban any American from claiming the citizenship of another country. He did not respond to a request for comment about Mace’s legislation. When I asked Mace about the fact that her proposal would block Moreno and other Republicans from serving, she said, “This isn’t personal. It’s about what standard we want for the people entrusted with enormous power over the American people.” T he Constitution already lays out specific qualifications for members of Congress, including a stipulation that any House member be at least 25 years old and have been a U.S. citizen for at least seven years. Any effort to add new requirements without amending the Constitution—as some of the recent proposals have attempted—would run into legal roadblocks, Pamela Karlan, a professor at Stanford Law School, told me. “Those qualifications are exclusive,” she said. “The state can’t add qualifications on top of those, nor indeed can the federal government.” After walking me through the nuances of the legal framework and the relevant case law, she offered a more frank perspective on the political backdrop that had made our conversation necessary in the first place: “It’s just incredibly ugly, stupid, and unconstitutional.” Judges have checked efforts to curb the rights of naturalized citizens; in the process, they’ve also become targets. When U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan ruled in June that the Trump administration had “knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens” with a federal database of citizenship information, her own citizenship status became an object of attack. Representative Abe Hamadeh of Arizona, a Republican, introduced articles of impeachment against Sooknanan, pointing out that the judge “holds dual citizenship in the United States and Trinidad and Tobago.” Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri, a Republican, wrote on X: “If judges can stop Presidents, they should not also be citizens of foreign nations.” Mace added, “No one born in another country should be serving in our government. Judges included.” Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, chimed in as well, sarcastically writing, “Judge Sparkle decrees that America belongs to any random alien on planet earth, just like our founders intended.” Miller has been a leading proponent of the idea that many of America’s modern-day problems can be traced back to its immigration policies. After Mamdani’s primary victory last year, Miller took to social media to decry how “unchecked migration fundamentally remade the NYC electorate,” branding New York “the clearest warning yet” of the downside of allowing so many foreigners into the country. Trump has also seized on the ascendance of Democratic Socialists of America–backed candidates such as Mamdani, linking their policies to communism and foreign ideology. With Miller’s help, he has implemented dozens of new restrictions on legal immigration, tightening virtually every avenue through which foreigners obtain visas and become Americans. The White House did not respond to a request for comment about whether the president supports barring naturalized citizens from public service and whether he agrees with lawmakers who are trying to do so. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order attempting to restrict birthright citizenship and warning about the “risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation.” Trump’s focus on such proposed risks echoes a sentiment that has become popular with his MAGA base: that America’s legal immigrants represent not, as the poet Emma Lazarus wrote, “huddled masses yearning to breathe free,” but instead national-security threats yearning to impose radical ideology on the masses already here. Muslim immigrants have received particular hostility. “We need more Islamophobia, not less,” Representative Randy Fine of Florida, a Republican, wrote on social media in March, a few months after he filed legislation to ban dual citizens from serving in Congress. “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,” Mace posted online earlier this month in response to the primary victory of the Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat. [ Read: Islamophobia has corroded American values ] Senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama, a Republican who is running for governor, took to the Senate floor last month to warn about Muslim immigrants, who, he said, are trying to “radically change the ethnic, religious, and political makeup of our country.” He declared that “Islam is not a religion; it’s a death cult.” In March, he reposted an image of Mamdani next to an image of the 9/11 attacks, declaring that the “enemy is inside the gates.” He has proposed the ASSIMILATION Act, which aims to impose new ideological restrictions on those seeking to become citizens. The bill has almost no chance of passing Congress, but Tuberville could have more success turning his ideas into legislation if, as expected, he wins his race for governor in November. He could also unstick efforts to block naturalized citizens from running for office in Alabama that stalled earlier this year. Former Representative Mo Brooks of Alabama, a Republican, told me that although he supports much of Trump’s immigration agenda, he opposes discriminating against U.S. citizens based on their place of birth. In a country that is growing more diverse, telling certain Americans that they should not be eligible to run for office is an easy way to ensure that they will never vote for your party, he said: “It is one of the dumbest tactical moves I’ve ever seen politicians make. It’s extraordinarily unwise to try to win elections based on this racist appeal.” There are more than 77,000 naturalized citizens in Alabama, accounting for 1.5 percent of the population, according to the American Immigration Council. With one of the lowest proportions of foreign-born residents in the country, the state is an odd place to be leading the charge against naturalized citizens in public service, Steven Taylor, a retired political-science professor at Troy University, told me. “On one level, it seems incredibly trivial,” he said. “On another, it seems kind of serious because of the ongoing, disturbing nationalism in our politics right now.” Alemán, who recently opted not to run for reelection to the Homewood City Council, told me that it is exhausting to constantly have his loyalty to America questioned. “My daughter has a southern twang. She pronounces words differently than I do. This is home to her,” he said, adding that he is proud that his children could see his community of mostly white residents choose him as their representative. “Alabama can surprise you sometimes.” If some policy makers have their way, the outcome could be surprising in a more alarming sense: Alemán’s children may grow up to see their father deemed American enough to vote, pay taxes, and raise a family here—but not American enough to serve as an elected official.

items.title: Federal Presence at US Polls Could Intimidate Voters
items.description: Click to expand Image Voters fill out their ballots at a polling station in New York City on Election Day, November 5, 2024. © 2024 Leonardo Munoz/ AFP via Getty Images The United States Justice Department announced plans earlier this month to deploy at least 1,000 federal officers to polling places during the upcoming midterm elections. While such deployments are not without precedent, federal officers previously deployed during elections have been tasked with enforcing federal statutes that protect the right to vote and prohibit voter intimidation and suppression. This time, the Trump administration has cast the effort in a manner that is likely to intimidate naturalized immigrant and non-English speaking communities. Letters sent to local officials warned that they face criminal charges for allowing non-citizens to vote, coinciding with the administration’s advancement of largely debunked claims of widespread non-citizen voting in US elections. US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of Homeland Security Markwayne Millin have also endorsed the notion of deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or other federal agents to polling locations. It is illegal under US law for federal agents to engage in voter intimidation. While the administration suggests that ICE deployment to polling stations will not affect eligible voters with legal status, there is ample reason to think otherwise. According to the ACLU, at least 155 US citizens across eight states in 2025, including 32 children, were either detained, targeted, or subjected to immigration enforcement misconduct, including use of force. In recent weeks, ICE agents have been present at a New York polling station and a constituent town hall held in Minnesota. The agency’s implication in numerous rights abuses aimed at protesters in recent months exacerbates the risk that the proposed federal presence at polling places could lead to voter intimidation. This is particularly true for non-white US voters, who are more likely to be stopped or detained by ICE. Local and state officials in the US should remain on high alert for voter intimidation and take measures to ensure every eligible voter has effective access to the democratic process—as required under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Other governments and international human rights mechanisms should condemn any efforts by the US government to intimidate voters or otherwise violate their rights.
